source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The episode is benign because the neurologic deficits resolved completely, so no urgent assessment is needed unless similar symptoms last longer the next time.","B":"The episode is most consistent with dehydration because transient focal weakness and dysarthria usually resolve after oral fluids without further evaluation.","C":"The episode can be managed as a routine outpatient complaint because transient neurologic symptoms do not meaningfully predict near-term stroke risk.","D":"The episode is consistent with a transient ischemic attack and requires urgent evaluation because transient symptoms can precede a completed ischemic stroke."}}
source_row.rationale: Sudden focal weakness and dysarthria that resolve can represent a TIA, and the American Stroke Association advises emergency assessment even when symptoms disappear. Option D correctly identifies both the syndrome and urgency. Option A wrongly treats symptom resolution as reassurance. Option B substitutes dehydration for a focal neurologic event without evidence. Option C understates the near-term stroke risk and delays evaluation.
source_row.source_detail: American Stroke Association — Transient Ischemic Attack: transient stroke-like focal neurologic symptoms may resolve but still require emergency assessment because TIA signals near-term stroke risk; comprehensive evaluation is recommended urgently.
